title: Elara and the Orb of Oopsies
markdown:
The last bell at Aethelred Academy was a friendly suggestion. Elara Pendelton treated it as optional. By the time the chime had gone into the oaks she was already halfway to the next class, which often meant she was halfway out of the present one. A lopsided biscuit shed crumbs down her chin. Her satchel beat a frantic time against her hip. Grammar-golems in the eaves chirped at stray commas and were ignored.

Aethelred sat in a valley where mist hugged the cobbles. Students learned to feel a lie in a sentence, to quiet a woolly beast, to hear what the woods did not say aloud. Elara was a scholarship pupil whose place still felt like a rumour that had come true. Her mind kept odd details the way pockets keep crumbs. Her punctuality was a myth even the Archive refused to invent.

She skidded past a prefect polishing a doorknob with a single swan feather and found Finnigan Croft in the main hall, leaning on a bookshelf as if boredom were a subject he had already passed. It was not that he did not care. He preferred not to be caught caring. His hazel eyes, inconveniently warm, tracked her anyway. He held a mug that smelled of actual peace.

“Morning, Elara,” he said, unhurried as water over stone.

“Finn. You will not believe this.” Words tumbled. The biscuit drew a crumb comet. “Truth and Tranquility. Professor Quill said capture genuine remorse and gently diffuse it. He had this orb. It shimmered. Then it poofed.”

Finn sipped. “A poofed orb. And you’re late for Potions.”

“I don’t think it poofed. I think it went out there.” She pointed at doors that opened onto Oakhaven’s ordinary lanes. “He said minor recalibration. His eyebrows did the jig that means the opposite.”

Finn set the mug down with a small, decisive thud. The blankness slipped. He always turned up. He always pretended he hadn’t meant to.

They found Professor Quill wringing his hands as if smoke could be folded. The air around him hummed like a harp strung wrong. A smear of pearly residue clung to his cuff like a tear that had forgotten to fall. “Elara. Finnigan. A kerfuffle. The essence of remorse has absconded. It was meant to be empathy in a jar. Collective regret from Oakhaven’s Forgot Your Anniversary day. Usually soothed by a lecture and daisies. This year it was… overcharged. Too much oopsie.”

Elara, who had arrived late, had missed the first half of that explanation and now ran to catch it, which was her habit in more than corridors. “Did it leave a trail? A colour? A smell? I read that residual regret sometimes—”

“It left a town,” Quill said, miserable and precise.

Finn picked up his mug again, then set it down unused. He had not been in the lesson. He was here anyway.

Outside, the town had gone peculiar. The baker, famed for a laugh that rose like good dough, cradled a slightly burnt scone. “The ignominy,” he whispered. “Every time I used too much yeast. The shame.”

Mrs Gable sat on her porch and wept at her prize petunias. “So alive. And I never looked. The injustice.”

Elara’s memory, which hoarded footnotes, clicked. Residual emotion. Last Tuesday’s regrettable moments, brought to class, amplified. “It’s making every slip feel like a tragedy.”

Finn watched a man sort pebbles by size as if the order might save him. “A broadcast of I-wish-I-hadn’t. Feeding itself.” He paused. “A feedback loop of oopsies.”

They followed the specific sadness down the high street and into the side lanes, where Oakhaven usually kept its smaller vanities. A man retying laces relived a trip from years ago, knot by knot. A woman mourned a gnome’s mushroom cap as if it were a crown. Two children sat on a stoop and apologised, in turns, for a broken chalk drawing that the rain had already forgiven. The baker’s scone held a faint electric-blue edge. The petunias wore a silvery cast, like moonlight that had lost its sense of humour.

Elara wanted to sprint to the square, invent a containment circle, and be done before Potions started without her. She took three fast steps. Finn did not match them. He stopped to look at a windowsill where a cat was washing one paw with ceremonial slowness, uninterested in the apocalypse of oopsies.

“If you run past it,” he said, “you’ll only be late to the important bit.”

That was the first hard corner: her lateness was not only clocks. It was leaving the actual problem one step behind her brilliance.

“Halo of hindsight,” Elara said, pleased with the phrase, and this time she stayed put long enough to see it on the scone, the flowers, the hanging water they had not reached yet. “Quill mentioned distortion. There’s a treatise.”

In a courtyard a forgotten fountain hung its water in the air for a breath, pearly, then let it fall. A cherub with a chipped mouth looked permanently surprised. Finn stopped. “Not just people. The place is getting melancholic.”

They stood there long enough for a pigeon to land, consider the mood, and leave. Stone. Drip. A town holding its breath. Elara felt the hush of it despite herself. Her satchel produced theories anyway: Emotional Resonance Chambers, counter-frequencies, a grand pure emotion to cancel gloom. She wanted a dash, a spell, something that would look like a scholarship well spent. The air thickened with wilting flowers and unsaid apologies. Quill hovered at the lane-end, a barometer of panic.

“We could overload it,” she said. “Joy. A lot of joy. I can fetch the choir.”

Finn’s mouth twitched. “The choir is currently weeping about a missed high note from Michaelmas.”

Finn was still at the cherub. A tiny moss bud clung to the stone wing and unfurled as if nobody had told it the town was ending.

“Look,” he said. “It’s just growing.”

Elara had a footnote for that too: Quill, week one, lichen on old stone, persistence so unassuming she had filed it under pointless. She had been late to that lecture as well, and remembered it anyway, which was the useful kind of lateness, if there was one.

The shining solution would have been a race. She left it. She took out her grandmother’s silver locket, a pressed forget-me-not inside, no fireworks in it. Remembering, not regretting. Being, not performing. The clasp stuck, because of course it did, and she had to stand there and work it with her thumbnail instead of inventing a better clasp.

She did not shout. She stood still, which cost her more than running. Finn stood with her, mug forgotten, a quiet weight on the afternoon. A drip from the cherub marked time better than Aethelred’s bell. She thought of the moss, of a warm biscuit that was allowed to be only a biscuit, of tea that did not have to apologise for existing. She thought of her grandmother’s kitchen, which had never been on time for anything except kindness. The locket stayed ordinary in her fist. The forget-me-not inside was brown at the edges and still, somehow, itself.

The fountain’s pearl-light ebbed. Water remembered how to splash. Somewhere a baker made a sound that was almost a chuckle. Mrs Gable wiped her eyes and looked at the petunias as if they were allowed to be flowers again. The pebble-sorter let his careful piles collapse and did not mourn them.

Quill whooped, then remembered dignity, then whooped smaller. “The unassuming anchor. Elara. And Finnigan, you stayed.”

Finn offered a nod you could miss if you were already late for the next wonder.

They walked back through a market that had recovered its colours without a speech about it. A stallholder offered Elara a spare bun and did not mention why. She ate it standing still, crumbs and all, which Finn observed as if it were advanced magic.

Elara was still going to be late for Potions. Finn, who pretended not to care, turned up at the classroom door with her biscuit crumbs still on his sleeve, and held it just long enough that Professor Quill’s eyebrows, for once, did not jig.
characters: Elara Pendelton (bright but chronically late scholarship pupil who has a sharp memory for odd details), Finn (a classmate who pretends not to care but always turns up)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, fantastic story for curious young teens
